title: Pritchett Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Pritchett wells have a 250-foot median depth; see local yields, water levels, drillers, and estimated finished-well costs.
h1: Pritchett, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Pritchett means looking past the presence of a well permit. The local records show 192 permitted wells within 8 miles, but only 105 are recorded as constructed. Depth, production, static water level, and intended use vary across this plains setting.

The useful starting point is a median depth of 250 feet, with the middle half between 180 and 301 feet. Reported yields have a median of 11.0 gallons per minute, though only 12 wells report a pump yield. Treat these figures as planning evidence, not a guarantee for a particular lot.

sections.heading: Pritchett well depths reflect plains sediments and bedrock
sections.html:
Recorded Pritchett-area wells have a median total depth of 250 feet. The middle half runs from 180 to 301 feet, while the 90th percentile is 380 feet. The deepest well in the records reaches 546 feet. Most are not shallow: 61% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and 33% are between 300 and 600 feet.

The permits name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers most often, followed by the Southern High Plains and Dakota aquifers. That mix helps explain why nearby parcels can require different drilling approaches. For a buyer, a bid based only on the average local depth is not enough. Ask the driller to price casing, grout, drilling conditions, and added footage if the target water-bearing zone is deeper than expected.

sections.heading: What Pritchett wells produce
sections.html:
The reported yield median is 11.0 gallons per minute, with a middle range of 9.0 to 240.0 gallons per minute. The distribution is favorable on paper: 50% of reported wells produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 42% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 8% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

Do not read that as a promise for a new hole. Only 12 wells in the records report a pump yield, and production depends on the formation encountered, completion, and testing method. Ask for the well construction report and a sustained pump test. A household-use exempt well is generally limited to 35 gallons per minute, and the permitted use matters because stock and irrigation wells make up much of this local record.

sections.heading: Pritchett water levels: useful baseline, limited trend
sections.html:
Seven Pritchett-area permits report a static water level. Their median depth to water is 159 feet, with the middle half between 106 and 214 feet. That is a practical baseline for estimating pump setting, trench planning, and electrical needs, but it is not the same as a guaranteed water level on an untested parcel.

The permit history does not provide enough reported static levels to establish a reliable decade-by-decade decline or rise. A buyer should therefore avoid assuming that the water table is stable or dropping based on this dataset alone. Check the nearest comparable wells, their completion aquifer, measured static levels, and any recent pump-test information before setting a budget or designing a pressure system.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Pritchett, and when
sections.html:
Pritchett has a long permit history. The records show 6 permits from the 1950s, 22 from the 1960s, 26 from the 1970s, 8 from the 1980s, 11 from the 1990s, 19 from the 2000s, 31 from the 2010s, and 8 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. That history shows continued drilling, not just an old rural water supply.

The most active named drillers in these records are Konkel Drilling, also listed as Konkel, David Leroy, with 19 wells; Hoffman, also listed as Hoffman, Earl, with 16; and Hegwood Drilling, also listed as Hegwood, Spencer, with 10. These records identify past activity, not a recommendation or proof of current availability. Confirm licensing, references, scheduling, and the proposed completion plan directly.

sections.heading: What a new well may cost near Pritchett
sections.html:
For Pritchett’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 250-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $8,800 to $13,800. A finished system, including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is estimated at $14,800 to $25,800.

That range is a budgeting tool, not a fixed quote. Depth is the main visible driver, but casing, grout, access, formation changes, pump size, power distance, and site trenching can move the final number. Get the drilling and completion assumptions in writing. Compare bids using the same target depth, testing, pump equipment, and electrical scope so a low initial price does not hide unfinished work.

sections.heading: Pritchett risks: low yield, contamination, and site layout
sections.html:
The largest practical risk is uncertainty, not a known pattern of failed wells. Only 12 permits report pump yield, and only 7 report static water level. Fractured-bedrock wells can be especially variable from parcel to parcel. A dry hole or weak producer is possible even where nearby records look good, so investigate neighboring construction reports before closing.

Environmental records within about 10 miles show 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site, with 0 historic mine features and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not certify a property’s water. Test an existing well for appropriate contaminants, inspect casing and grout, and keep the well separated from septic components. Septic design, driveway access, house location, and utility trenching should be planned together before drilling.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Pritchett
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado Division of Water Resources permit and construction records for the exact parcel and nearby wells. Confirm the permit’s allowed use: local records are 62% stock, 20% irrigation, 15% domestic or household, and 6% monitoring. A stock or irrigation permit may not support the household use you expect. Exempt household-use wells also have specific limits, including the 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

For a vacant lot, obtain a written drilling estimate based on the local 180-to-301-foot middle range, but carry allowance for a deeper completion up to the 380-foot 90th percentile and beyond. Verify septic feasibility, access for a rig, electrical distance, and water testing before purchase deadlines. If the basin or proposed use requires more water than the permit allows, ask about augmentation requirements early.

faq.q: How deep are wells near Pritchett, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within 8 miles of Pritchett is 250 feet. The middle half runs from 180 to 301 feet, 61% are between 100 and 300 feet, and 33% are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 546 feet, so a particular parcel can require substantially more drilling.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Pritchett?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 250-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $8,800 to $13,800. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $14,800 to $25,800. Actual bids depend on depth, casing, grout, access, formation, and power distance.

faq.q: How much water do wells near Pritchett produce?
faq.a: Reported well yields have a median of 11.0 gallons per minute, with a middle range of 9.0 to 240.0 gallons per minute. Half of reported wells produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 42% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 12 wells report a pump yield, so these figures do not guarantee a new well’s production.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink near Pritchett?
faq.a: The records show 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site within about 10 miles, with 0 historic mine features and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That regional information cannot certify an individual well. Test existing or newly completed wells, inspect casing and grout, and consider the property’s distance from septic systems and the mapped PFAS site.

faq.q: Can I use a Pritchett well for a new home?
faq.a: That depends on the permit’s authorized use and the property’s water-rights requirements. Nearby records are 62% stock, 20% irrigation, 15% domestic or household, and 6% monitoring, so not every well supports a residence. Confirm the DWR permit, household-use limits, septic feasibility, and any augmentation requirement before buying or building.
